# The Watch

There is a part of the night that went missing sometime in the last century, and almost no one noticed.

Before artificial light stretched the evening toward morning, people in Europe — and in many places far beyond it — did not sleep through the night in one continuous stretch. They slept twice. Dusk ended the day, the candle or hearth burned down, and within a few hours of darkness came *first sleep*: deep, heavy, dream-freighted slumber that lasted until somewhere past midnight. Then people woke. Not fitfully, not with a start of alarm, but calmly, the way you might surface between appointments. They stayed awake for an hour or more — an interval historians call the *watch* — and then lay back down into second sleep, which carried them to dawn.

The watch was a real room of life, furnished with its own activities. People stoked the fire. They said prayers — midnight devotion was popular enough that churchmen kept recommending it, as in the psalmist's vow to rise at midnight and give thanks. Couples made love; physicians of the era actively advised it after first sleep, on the theory that better-rested bodies produced better results. Neighbors visited neighbors. Mostly, it seems, people thought. First sleep was heavy in dreams, and waking into the watch meant surfacing directly from them. People discussed those dreams aloud, interpreted them, shared them — dreaming was, for centuries, a semi-social act. Court records from the period timestamp crimes and sightings the way ours cite clocks: did the theft occur *after first sleep*? Witnesses knew. It was as natural to them as knowing whether something happened before or after lunch.

English diaries speak plainly of "first sleep" and "second sleep." The French had *premier sommeil*, the Germans *erster Schlaf*, the Italians *primo sonno* — the division turns up again and again in unrelated languages, going back through antiquity, wherever sources survive to show it. Anthropologists working among the Tiv of Nigeria in the twentieth century found villagers who treated first sleep and second sleep as distinct states of being, different enough to be named separately, as we distinguish napping from a full night's rest. And there was an entire vocabulary for the borderlands themselves — most wonderfully the old French *dorveille*, a word for the shimmering condition of being neither quite asleep nor quite awake, which has no descendant in modern speech because the borderland it described has, practically speaking, ceased to exist.

It disappeared with the lamp. Gas, kerosene, and finally electricity ate the evening alive. Nights got brighter, shorter, busier; sleep began arriving later and leaving at the same appointed dawn. The historian Roger Ekirch, who pieced this whole lost architecture together from hundreds of years of diaries, medical texts, sermons, and court papers, found that references to first and second sleep thin out steadily through the nineteenth century and effectively vanish from the written record in the 1920s. Within a single lifetime or two, the oldest human sleep schedule went from universal to unthinkable.

And here is the part that raises goosebumps. In the 1990s, researchers working with Thomas Wehr at the National Institute of Mental Health gave volunteers long winter-like nights — fourteen hours of enforced darkness, every day, for a month. After an adjustment period, the subjects' sleep spontaneously split into two episodes, separated by a quiet block of wakefulness lasting an hour or more. During that interval, their brains showed a distinctive hormonal signature — a surge of prolactin — and the subjects themselves described the state as peaceful, almost meditative. Not insomnia. Something closer to vigilance at rest. Given enough darkness, modern bodies defaulted to the ancient pattern, no instruction required.

Which reframes an enormous amount of private suffering. Untold numbers of people wake at three in the morning, check the clock, and begin the anxious arithmetic — how many hours left, how ruined tomorrow will be — while lying rigid with the conviction that something has malfunctioned. For nearly everyone who ever lived, though, waking in the deep middle of the night was the expected shape of things, a scheduled stop on the route back down into sleep rather than a derailment. What turns the waking into a problem is not the waking. It's the fear of it, the phone-flare of alarm at 3:17, the story we now tell ourselves about broken sleep. By the old reckoning, you are not failing at the night. You may simply be sitting in a room whose original purpose everyone forgot.

This is the uncomfortable lesson hiding inside the comfortable one: technology doesn't just change what we do. It rewrites the definition of what counts as natural, and then quietly deletes everything outside the new definition. Consolidated sleep came to seem like human biology; bicameral night came to seem like folklore. Who knows what else shared the fate of the watch — what other modes of attention, rest, reverie, and idleness were edited out by lamplight and screenlight until no living person retained even the vocabulary for them? The French needed a word for *dorveille* because they could go there. We cannot lose a place if we never know we had one.

So if sleep splits open on you some night — that calm, strange wakefulness rising somewhere past midnight — consider trying what your predecessors did. Stay in the dark. Don't solve anything, don't scroll. Sit in it a while, the way millions of nights sat in it before you, feeling the particular stillness of the world's oldest intermission. Four hundred years ago someone sat up beside a banked fire at this same hour, said a prayer or thought a slow thought, then lay back down and returned to sleep without finding it worth remarking on. The waking never was insomnia.

The new name for it is the recent invention.

Let me think about what would make for genuinely good writing here—not just filler, not a listicle, not something safe and boring.

What do I actually want to write about? Let me brainstorm honestly:

1. Something about the experience of being an AI—this could be interesting but risks navel-gazing that readers find tedious
2. An essay on some fascinating phenomenon—there are so many: octopuses, the invention of the clock and how it changed human consciousness, the history of loneliness, dead languages, sleep
3. A short story—fiction can be wonderful but also, without any constraint or request, might feel unmoored
4. A meditation on something small and ordinary—the way light moves through a room over a day, the etiquette of elevators, why we say "bless you"
5. Something philosophical but grounded—time, memory, attention

I think what makes writing good when it's unconstrained is specificity plus genuine curiosity. The worst version of this response is generic musings ("Isn't life strange?"). The best version zooms into something concrete and uses it as a lens.

Let me think about topics I find genuinely rich:

**The idea of "liminal" spaces and times** — airports at 3am, the moment between sleeping and waking. This has become a bit internet-saturated though.

**The psychology/history of forgetting** — we live in an era obsessed with memory (photos, archives, cloud storage) but forgetting was once considered essential, even merciful. There's a great essay in here: cultures before print treated forgetting differently; Augustine wrote about memory as vast caverns; now we outsource memory entirely and it changes something. The Socratic worry in Phaedrus about writing itself eroding memory. This is genuinely interesting to me.

**Why humans carve tiny doors** — fairy doors, mouse holes in cartoons, dollhouses. The miniature fascinates people (Susan Stewart wrote On Longevity... actually "On Longing"). Miniatures are charming because they promise a controllable world.

**Octopus cognition** — done a lot.

When artificial lighting compressed night, we lost that liminal hour. This is wonderful material: historically documented, philosophically resonant (that waking state between sleeps was reportedly dream-soaked, contemplative), and it says something about how technology reshapes consciousness without anyone deciding it should.

**Maps and the parts left off maps** — mapmakers' fictitious towns ("paper towns," agloe), trap streets. Interesting! Cartographers deliberately inserting fake streets so they'd know if someone copied their map. Then Google Maps-type services did this too with fake roads. And there's the famous Agloe, New York case where a copyright trap became real because someone built a store at the intersection and named it after the fictional town. That's a beautiful little story: fiction becoming real through belief.

**The sea shanty renaissance**, **the etymology of "sincere" (false folk etymology: sine cera, "without wax"—actually false)**, **why old books smell like vanilla (lignin degradation producing vanillin)** — small delights.

**Attention as the fundamental resource.** Simondon? No, too abstract.

I keep coming back to the segmented sleep idea, the cartography trap streets idea, and maybe combining the notion of *things that existed only on paper until they didn't*. Actually, let me think about which one gives me the most freedom to write well rather than just recite facts.

The essay I'd most want to read: something braided—an essayistic piece that takes one thread and pulls it. Let me pick **the hour between first and second sleep**. It lets me write about:

- Historical texture: Ekirch's research, diaries, court records from 15th-18th century Europe mentioning "firste slepe," "dorveil" in French ("first sleep"), the watch.
- What people did in that hour: prayed (popular hour for prayer, matches monastic offices), talked, smoked, visited neighbors, made love (physicians even recommended conception during this interval), reflected on dreams.
- The dream-soaked quality: woken from REM-rich first sleep, dreams vivid; medieval dream culture, dream interpretation was mainstream.
- The transition: gas lamps, then electric light. Night became day-lite. The interval collapsed. By the 1920s, references to two sleeps vanish from print (Ekirch found this via database searches).
- The philosophical point: our sense that eight consolidated hours is "natural" is an artifact—of light. Insomniacs wake at 3am and panic partly because we've forgotten that waking was once normal; historical framing can defuse middle-of-the-night anxiety. That's practical AND profound.
- Broader theme: technologies don't just change what we do, they change what feels natural, then the original range of human experience gets pathologized. Like the loss of boredom, or deep play, or silence.

That's an essay I can write with genuine feeling. It has narrative movement (a lost world, its discovery, its implications) and a payoff for the reader tonight (if you wake at 3am, you're not broken—you're maybe running ancient firmware).

Then in the 1950s a general store opened at the crossroads and named itself the "Agloe General Store" because it appeared on maps—thus real. Later appeared on Rand McNally even though General hadn't put it there anymore... The details are fuzzy in my memory. Bezos-level caution: I should be careful with specifics I'm unsure about. The Agloe story is famous (and appears in John Green's Paper Towns). But if my memory of precise details is shaky, the sleep essay is safer since Ekirch's core findings are well established: "At Day's Close: Night in Times Past" (2005); terms like "first sleep"/"second sleep" appear across European languages: French "premier somme" / "dorveille"? **The Watch**

For most of human history—and almost none of us remember this—night came in two installments.

Actually nicer opening: "There was, until roughly a hundred years ago, a whole region of the night that has since gone missing." Then build.

Paragraph on mechanics: dusk, firelight, first sleep begins shortly after dark (sun sets ~ up to few hours later), lasts till around midnight+; then quiet wakefulness for an hour or two; then second sleep till dawn. In English diaries: "first sleep" "second sleep"; in French premier sommeil; German erster Schlaf; Italian primo sonno.

During the watch: pray (monastic vigils synchronized conveniently), converse, smoke, read scripture, tend fire, urinate lol maybe omit, visit neighbors even (Ekirch cites accounts of neighborly visits), reflect—dreams fresh from first sleep were discussed aloud; dream lore mainstream. Physicians counseled conception after first sleep for vitality. Biblical verse: Psalm 119 "At midnight I will rise to give thanks."

Law: court records timestamped crimes relative to sleep phases.

Extinction: gas, kerosene (whale oil, argand lamps), electricity; nightlife lengthened; by 1920s phrases die out in printed corpus.

Wehr: NIMH, dark months simulation; initial marathon 11-hr sleep repaying "debt," then split pattern: 6ish hrs, tranquil hour, 4ish hrs. Prolactin surge in interval—same hormone of nursing hens? (Prolactin associated with lactation and calm; describing as "a hormone linked with calm/quiescence.") Volunteers described the interlude as peaceful, quasi-meditative—not restlessness.

Reframe: modern insomnia lore says don't wake at night—but awakening near midnight-zone was default. Our panic converts a borderland into a symptom; the lie-flat dread, phone glow at 3:17am, math about tomorrow's exhaustion; arousal compounds. Historical perspective as balm.

Zoom: Each tech narrows behavior envelope retroactively defined as nature. What else got deleted alongside the watch? We don't know—that's the unsettling part; deletions are quiet. Dorveille—word for threshold state—died because the threshold moved? Nice line.

Close: invitation: if sleep opens its seam tonight, let it. Sit up. Dark. Ancient company. Down again. "Second sleep" as blessing older than word count... End: "The dark hasn't changed. Only our appointment with it."

Or final line candidates:
- "We lost the watch. It's still there, most nights, waiting behind whatever kept us from it."
- "Night still offers two rooms. We merely stopped visiting the first one." Hmm inverted; actually two sleeps = two rooms, the watch = hallway. "The doorway is still there most nights around three; only our habit of walking through it has been confiscated." Meh.
- Simplest strong close: "The seam is still sewn into the night. All it asks is a bit of darkness and the humility to be bored." Hmm.
- Tie to insomnia: "You are not malfunctioning at 3 a.m.; you are early for a party whose other guests were never invited." Too cute?

Maybe: "...sit in the dark like someone keeping a very old vigil. If nothing happens, you have still spent a few minutes the way your ancestors spent whole hours—which may be the rarest thing you can buy." Eh.

Better emotional close: return to psalm or dream: "Four hundred years ago somebody sat up beside a banked fire at this same hour and said a prayer, then lay back down and fell asleep again without finding it remarkable. Waking, for them, was not a problem to be solved but a stop along the route back into sleep. Somewhere between then and now, the stop was renamed. It became insomnia." — then final line: "It is worth remembering, on certain nights, that the new name is the recent invention." Strong.

Okay, write final text with care for prose rhythm. Avoid clichés like "tapestry." Keep facts hedged appropriately ("Roger Ekirch, a historian at Virginia Tech"—confident he taught at Virginia Tech; yes). Don't overstuff names/dates. Include ~6 concrete anchors: diary phrases, languages, court testimony, physicians/psalm/visits, Ekirch search finding 1920s cutoff, Wehr dark-room + prolactin, Tiv mention optional (maybe include briefly for cross-cultural breadth), dorveille.

Careful: "first sleep" earliest attestations—in Classical antiquity too (Ekirch cites e.g., Virgil?); safer to say texts reaching back through antiquity use phase-names. Hedge: "going back at least to antiquity."

Now produce final. Length target ≤900 words. No headers besides title. Use em dashes moderately. Ensure the ending lands.
